headline: SOFTWARE
WITH A SPINE
hero.dek: Local engineer Joaquín Godoy observed wiring machines to speak plainly. Witnesses report entire systems “explaining themselves” without supervision. The engineer insists the feat owes much to a peculiar contrivance he calls “Artificial Intelligence” — whatever that may be.
hero.byline: BY OUR TECHNOLOGY CORRESPONDENT — WIRED FROM THE SCENE
paragraphs: Mr. Godoy makes no secret of his enthusiasm. The thinking machine, he declares, is the greatest alteration to his trade in a generation, and he will say so at length to anyone who calls. Your correspondent, who had come prepared for the usual denials, found him instead at a side bench of the workshop, sleeves up, arguing with the apparatus.

He grants its faults readily. It will produce a hundred pages before breakfast and answer for none of them; it has no name upon the work and no cause ever to return. He does not appear to regard this as reason to set it aside — only as reason to remain in the room. Responsibility, he holds, has not yet been mechanised, and until it is, the engineer’s signature is the only one on the drawing. (Consulted upon the point, the apparatus offered several opinions and settled upon none.)

The rest is a matter of what the contrivance is fed. His preference runs to machinery that will stand upright: readable in the morning, honest under load, and unbowed by the fashions of the season. A machine of good posture, he observes, the new apparatus may be trusted with. A machine of poor posture it will simply build wrong, and faster.
Beauty, he maintains, is of little use unless the machinery continues to behave when no one is watching.

Callers describe ledgers reconciling themselves, queries confessing their cost before execution, and entire systems reporting their ailments in plain language. The result is machinery built not merely to function, but to endure inspection, alteration, and the occasional indignity of being inherited by another man.

profile.title: An Account of the Subject, in Four Parts

parts.title: Foundations.
parts.body: His trade began, as such things often do, with curiosity. Taking systems apart, tracing their workings, and wondering why some machines endured while others collapsed beneath their own cleverness.
parts.tight: The habit, it is said, never quite left him.

parts.title: Practice.
parts.body: Godoy works chiefly by subtraction. He favours plain structures, legible code, and tools that earn their place. New machinery is welcomed when it shortens the road, but never when it obscures where the road leads.

parts.title: Principles.
parts.body: He has little patience for complexity without cause, ornament without purpose, or contraptions their maker cannot explain. Software, he maintains, ought to be useful, understandable, and built to survive the hands that come after his own.

parts.kicker: PART IV — OF THE MAN HIMSELF
parts.title: Elsewhere.
parts.body: Away from the workshop, the subject’s curiosities range considerably farther afield. He may be found wandering invented worlds, following public affairs with perhaps too much attention, losing an evening to music or a book, or pursuing some entirely unnecessary question simply because it caught his interest.
parts.tight: By all accounts, the machinery is only part of the man.
